claim: Patients' colorectal tumors have significantly higher heterogeneity of energy metabolism compared with cultured cells and tumor xenografts.
source: Our results demonstrate that patients' colorectal tumors have significantly higher heterogeneity of energy metabolism compared with cultured cells and tumor xenografts, which was displayed as a wider and frequently bimodal distribution of a contribution of a free (glycolytic) fraction of NAD(P)H within a sample.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding based on FLIM measurements comparing different model systems.

claim: Higher heterogeneity in patients' tumors was displayed as a wider and frequently bimodal distribution of a contribution of a free (glycolytic) fraction of NAD(P)H within a sample.
source: Our results demonstrate that patients' colorectal tumors have significantly higher heterogeneity of energy metabolism compared with cultured cells and tumor xenografts, which was displayed as a wider and frequently bimodal distribution of a contribution of a free (glycolytic) fraction of NAD(P)H within a sample.
evidence: The abstract describes the specific manifestation of metabolic heterogeneity observed in the data.

claim: Among patients' tumors, the dispersion was larger in the high-grade and early stage ones.
source: Among patients' tumors, the dispersion was larger in the high-grade and early stage ones, without, however, any association with bimodality.
evidence: The abstract reports findings from statistical analysis of patient tumor data.

claim: There is no association between dispersion and bimodality in patients' tumors.
source: Among patients' tumors, the dispersion was larger in the high-grade and early stage ones, without, however, any association with bimodality.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the lack of association between these two metrics.

claim: Cell-level metabolic heterogeneity assessed from NAD(P)H FLIM has a potential to become a clinical prognostic factor.
source: These results indicate that cell-level metabolic heterogeneity assessed from NAD(P)H FLIM has a potential to become a clinical prognostic factor.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this interpretation based on the associations found with clinical parameters.

claim: Tumor cells adjust their metabolism to sustain uncontrolled proliferation and tumor progression, even in the conditions of low nutrient supply and hypoxia.
source: Tumor cells adjust their metabolism to sustain uncontrolled proliferation and tumor progression, even in the conditions of low nutrient supply and hypoxia.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Enhanced glycolysis has been considered as a central feature of tumor metabolism.
source: For a long time, enhanced glycolysis has been considered as a central feature of tumor metabolism (DeBerardinis and Chandel, 2016).
evidence: This is cited as established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Tumor cells rely on glycolysis not only in hypoxia (anaerobic glycolysis), but also in normoxia (aerobic glycolysis, or the Warburg effect).
source: Unlike most normal cells, tumor cells rely on glycolysis not only in hypoxia (anaerobic glycolysis), but also in normoxia (aerobic glycolysis, or the Warburg effect), which provides them with many metabolic intermediates and a high-speed production of ATP for fast growth.
evidence: This describes the Warburg effect as established knowledge.

claim: The glycolytic shift in the tumors traditionally correlates with negative prognosis.
source: The glycolytic shift in the tumors traditionally correlates with negative prognosis (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as an established correlation.

claim: Mitochondrial OXPHOS is as important in malignant cells as glycolysis.
source: At the same time, mitochondrial OXPHOS is as important in malignant cells as glycolysis.
evidence: This is stated as current understanding in the field.

claim: Many tumors preserve functional mitochondria and normal OXPHOS rate.
source: Although defective mitochondria and lower OXPHOS capacity are often observed in cancer cells, this is not an absolute phenomenon – many tumors preserve functional mitochondria and normal OXPHOS rate (Gentric et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Tumor cells are capable of switching between different metabolic pathways depending on their own needs and local environment.
source: Interestingly, tumor cells are capable of switching between different metabolic pathways depending on their own needs and local environment, thus demonstrating a high degree of metabolic plasticity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about tumor metabolism.

claim: Intratumor heterogeneity means that there are the cells with different metabolic profiles in a tumor concurrently.
source: In this context, intratumor heterogeneity means that there are the cells with different metabolic profiles in a tumor concurrently, and intertumor heterogeneity means that tumors of the same type and stage are characterized by the different metabolic strategies (Kim and DeBerardinis, 2019).
evidence: This is a definition cited from the literature.

claim: Intertumor heterogeneity means that tumors of the same type and stage are characterized by the different metabolic strategies.
source: In this context, intratumor heterogeneity means that there are the cells with different metabolic profiles in a tumor concurrently, and intertumor heterogeneity means that tumors of the same type and stage are characterized by the different metabolic strategies (Kim and DeBerardinis, 2019).
evidence: This is a definition cited from the literature.

claim: Metabolic heterogeneity as a part of general heterogeneity of tumors imposes some difficulties in patients' diagnosis and treatment and is believed to have a prognostic value.
source: Collectively, these factors lead to variability of tumor metabolism in space and time. Metabolic heterogeneity as a part of general heterogeneity of tumors imposes some difficulties in patients' diagnosis and treatment and is believed to have a prognostic value (Liu et al., 2022a; Liu et al., 2022b; Pinho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as an established view.

claim: Clinical imaging modalities, such as metabolic PET with radiolabeled tracers (18F, 11C) and MRI/MRS, allow to capture inter- and intratumor heterogeneity among patients with low (~4.5 mm) spatial resolution.
source: Clinical imaging modalities, such as metabolic PET with radiolabeled tracers (18F, 11C) and MRI/MRS, allow to capture inter- and intratumor heterogeneity among patients with low (~4.5 mm) spatial resolution (Plathow and Weber, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from the literature describing existing methods.

claim: Methods of single-cell sequencing deliver comprehensive information about the metabolic landscape of a tumor with a resolution up to 55–100 µm based on the expression of the metabolic genes.
source: Recently evolved methods of single-cell sequencing deliver comprehensive information about the metabolic landscape of a tumor with a resolution up to 55–100 µm based on the expression of the metabolic genes, but these approaches are rather complex, laborious and not widely available (Evers et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the literature describing existing methods.

claim: The unbound state of NAD(P)H has a short lifetime (~0.4 ns), while the protein-bound state has a long lifetime (~1.7–3.0 ns).
source: The unbound state of NAD(P)H has a short lifetime (~0.4 ns), while the protein-bound state has a long lifetime (~1.7–3.0 ns; Lakowicz et al., 1992).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as established knowledge about NAD(P)H fluorescence properties.

claim: Changes in the relative fractions of the unbound and bound NAD(P)H in cancer cells calculated from biexponential fitting of decay curve typically indicate the shifts between glycolysis and OXPHOS.
source: Changes in the relative fractions of the unbound and bound NAD(P)H in cancer cells calculated from biexponential fitting of decay curve typically indicate the shifts between glycolysis and OXPHOS (Rück et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as an established interpretation of FLIM data.

claim: Typical values of NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetimes were registered for all cell lines – short τ1~0.39 ns and long τ2~2.03–2.59 ns.
source: Typical values of NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetimes were registered for all cell lines – short τ1~0.39 ns and long τ2~2.03–2.59 ns (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results section and Table 1.

claim: The a1 value decreased and τm increased in the following order: CT26 (~86%, 0.57 ns)>HCT116 (~84%, 0.71 ns)>HT29 (~80%, 0.80 ns)>CaCo2 (~73%, 0.95 ns).
source: The a1 value decreased and τm increased in the following order: CT26 (~86%, 0.57 ns)>HCT116 (~84%, 0.71 ns)>HT29 (~80%, 0.80 ns)>CaCo2 (~73%, 0.95 ns) (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results section with reference to Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: A high NAD(P)H-a1 (low τm) is an indicator of glycolytic shift, which is typical for cells with intense proliferation in a monolayer culture, like CT26 and HCT116.
source: A high NAD(P)H-a1 (low τm) is an indicator of glycolytic shift, which is typical for cells with intense proliferation in a monolayer culture, like CT26 and HCT116.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on established knowledge about NAD(P)H FLIM parameters.

claim: CaCo2 cells with the lowest a1 value had more OXPHOS-shifted metabolism, which can be associated with the expression of morphological and functional characteristics of mature enterocytes of normal small intestine by this cell line.
source: CaCo2 cells with the lowest a1 value had more OXPHOS-shifted metabolism, which can be associated with the expression of morphological and functional characteristics of mature enterocytes of normal small intestine by this cell line (Lea, 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with a citation supporting the biological context.

claim: All cell lines statistically differed from each other in NAD(P)H-a1 values.
source: All cell lines statistically differed from each other (for p-val, see Supplementary file 1), and intercellular variations of the a1 parameter were minor (<3%).
evidence: This is a statistical finding reported in the results.

claim: Intercellular variations of the a1 parameter were minor (<3%) in cell lines.
source: All cell lines statistically differed from each other (for p-val, see Supplementary file 1), and intercellular variations of the a1 parameter were minor (<3%).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results.

claim: For all cell lines the BI of the a1 distribution did not exceed 1.1, justifying the uniformity of cell metabolism in a culture.
source: For all cell lines the BI of the a1 distribution did not exceed 1.1 (the threshold of bimodality, Wang et al., 2009), justifying the uniformity of cell metabolism in a culture, which is consistent with the general view on standard cell lines as homogenous populations (Auman and McLeod, 2010; Idrisova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis with citations supporting the interpretation.

claim: The BI ≥1.1 is considered as a cutoff to reliably define a bimodal distribution in the data.
source: For all cell lines the BI of the a1 distribution did not exceed 1.1 (the threshold of bimodality, Wang et al., 2009), justifying the uniformity of cell metabolism in a culture, which is consistent with the general view on standard cell lines as homogenous populations (Auman and McLeod, 2010; Idrisova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as an established threshold.

claim: Standard cell lines are generally viewed as homogenous populations.
source: For all cell lines the BI of the a1 distribution did not exceed 1.1 (the threshold of bimodality, Wang et al., 2009), justifying the uniformity of cell metabolism in a culture, which is consistent with the general view on standard cell lines as homogenous populations (Auman and McLeod, 2010; Idrisova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from the literature as established knowledge.

claim: Among the tumors, CT26 had the highest (~82%), and CaCo2 had, on average, the lowest (~76%, p-val=0.0028) contribution of free NAD(P)H a1.
source: Among the tumors, CT26 had the highest (~82%), and CaCo2 had, on average, the lowest (~76%, p-val=0.0028) contribution of free NAD(P)H a1, similar to the cultured cells (Figure 2C, Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results with statistical significance.

claim: Most of the individual tumors showed larger (≥3%) inter-cellular variations of NAD(P)H-a1 than corresponding cell lines, where the deviation from the median was ≤3%.
source: Most of the individual tumors showed larger (≥3%) inter-cellular variations of NAD(P)H-a1 than corresponding cell lines, where the deviation from the median was ≤3%.
evidence: This is a comparison of measurements between cell lines and tumors.

claim: The dispersion D-a1 was in the range of 2.6–4.0% in mouse tumors.
source: The dispersion D-a1 was in the range of 2.6–4.0% (Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results.

claim: Intertumor differences across each type of tumor were insignificant.
source: At that, intertumor differences across each type of tumor were insignificant.
evidence: This is a statistical finding reported in the results.

claim: In 5 of 19 tumors the BI-a1 was ≥1.1, indicating the bimodal distribution of the a1 parameter.
source: In 5 of 19 tumors the BI-a1 was ≥1.1, indicating the bimodal distribution of the a1 parameter, that is the presence of two subpopulations of cells with different metabolism.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Ten tumors had the BI-a1 in the range of 0.7–1.0, which suggests that, while the distribution of the estimated parameter was unimodal, it was either wide or asymmetric.
source: Ten tumors had the BI-a1 in the range of 0.7–1.0, which suggests that, while the distribution of the estimated parameter was unimodal, it was either wide or asymmetric, thus, also indicating some degree of heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis with interpretation.

claim: In 4 of 19 tumors the BI-a1 was small (0.43–0.69), suggesting uniformity of cells' metabolism.
source: In 4 of 19 tumors the BI-a1 was small (0.43–0.69), suggesting uniformity of cells' metabolism.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis with interpretation.

claim: The nonuniform microenvironment in the tumors was a major source of their variable metabolism.
source: Given the genetic identity of cells in standard cell lines, we can assume that the nonuniform microenvironment in the tumors was a major source of their variable metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and knowledge about cell line genetics.

claim: Patients' tumors showed fluorescence lifetimes of τ1~0.45 ns and τ2~1.80–3.20 ns.
source: Patients' tumors showed fluorescence lifetimes of τ1~0.45 ns and τ2~1.80–3.20 ns (Supplementary file 2), which were comparable with the values in human tumor xenografts (Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results.

claim: The parameter NAD(P)H-a1 was in the range of ~62–80% and NAD(P)H-τm was in the range of 0.80–1.20 ns in patients' tumors.
source: The parameter NAD(P)H-a1 was in the range of ~62–80% and NAD(P)H-τm was in the range of 0.80–1.20 ns, indicating that patients' tumors generally had larger variability of metabolic statuses than cancer cells in vitro and in xenografts in vivo.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results with interpretation.

claim: Patients' tumors generally had larger variability of metabolic statuses than cancer cells in vitro and in xenografts in vivo.
source: The parameter NAD(P)H-a1 was in the range of ~62–80% and NAD(P)H-τm was in the range of 0.80–1.20 ns, indicating that patients' tumors generally had larger variability of metabolic statuses than cancer cells in vitro and in xenografts in vivo.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing different model systems.

claim: Less than half of the tumors (13 of 29) showed deviation of NAD(P)H-a1 from the median <10% across the cells.
source: Less than half of the tumors (13 of 29) showed deviation of NAD(P)H-a1 from the median <10% across the cells, and for the rest (16 of 29) the variations were 10–25%.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: For 16 of 29 patient tumors, the variations of NAD(P)H-a1 were 10–25%.
source: Less than half of the tumors (13 of 29) showed deviation of NAD(P)H-a1 from the median <10% across the cells, and for the rest (16 of 29) the variations were 10–25%.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The dispersion D-a1 varied significantly among the patient samples, from 2.19% to 11.99%.
source: The dispersion D-a1 varied significantly among the samples, from 2.19% to 11.99%.
evidence: This is a direct measurement reported in the results.

claim: 14 of 29 patient tumors were metabolically highly heterogeneous (BI-a1 ≥1.1).
source: According to the heterogeneity assessment using the bimodality index, 14 of 29 tumors were metabolically highly heterogeneous (BI-a1 ≥1.1) (Figure 3D, Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: In 14 patient tumors the BI-a1 value was in the range of 0.50–1.0, which indicated the presence of metabolically different cells but not clearly separated into two clusters.
source: In 14 tumors the BI-a1 value was in the range of 0.50–1.0, which indicated the presence of metabolically different cells but not clearly separated into two clusters.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis with interpretation.

claim: Only one tumor sample (p16) was metabolically homogeneous (BI-a1=0.24).
source: Only one tumor sample (p16) was metabolically homogeneous (BI-a1=0.24).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The bimodality index showed no correlation with dispersion.
source: Notably, the bimodality index showed no correlation with dispersion.
evidence: This is a statistical finding reported in the results.

claim: Among the samples there were those with bimodal distribution, but small dispersion of NAD(P)H-a1 in a cell population (e.g. samples № 12, 13, 21).
source: That is, among the samples there were those with bimodal distribution, but small dispersion of NAD(P)H-a1 in a cell population (e.g. samples № 12, 13, 21), and vice versa (e.g. samples № 3, 7, 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis illustrating the lack of correlation.

claim: Among the samples there were those with large dispersion but not bimodal distribution (e.g. samples № 3, 7, 8).
source: That is, among the samples there were those with bimodal distribution, but small dispersion of NAD(P)H-a1 in a cell population (e.g. samples № 12, 13, 21), and vice versa (e.g. samples № 3, 7, 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis illustrating the lack of correlation.

claim: Patients' tumors are genetically diverse, which could contribute to their metabolic heterogeneity, in addition to microenvironmental factors.
source: Unlike tumor xenografts obtained from the cell lines that are thought to be genetically stable and identical, patients' tumors are genetically diverse, which could also contribute to their metabolic heterogeneity, in addition to microenvironmental factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about tumor biology.

claim: Among the variables, dispersion of a1 had a major relative weight in the prediction of all the clinical characteristics studied.
source: The results showed that, among the variables, dispersion of a1 had a major relative weight in the prediction of all the clinical characteristics studied.
evidence: This is a finding from the SHAP analysis.

claim: The tumors of the advanced stages T3 and T4 were characterized by reduced dispersion of a1 compared with early stages T1 and T2.
source: The tumors of the advanced stages T3 and T4 were characterized by reduced dispersion of a1 compared with early stages T1 and T2, indicating their lower heterogeneity (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The stage of the tumor T was significantly associated with the value of D-a1 (p-val=0.02).
source: The stage of the tumor T was significantly associated with the value of D-a1 (p-val=0.02).
evidence: This is a statistical finding reported in the results.

claim: If metastases were present (N and M were different from 0 in TNM), then those primary tumors showed a tendency to have lower D-a1 compared with tumors for which metastases were absent (p-val=0.056).
source: If metastases were present (N and M were different from 0 in TNM), then those primary tumors showed a tendency to have lower D-a1 compared with tumors for which metastases were absent (p-val=0.056).
evidence: This is a statistical finding reported in the results.

claim: The high-grade tumors displayed a higher value of dispersion D-a1 than the low-grade ones.
source: The high-grade tumors displayed a higher value of dispersion D-a1 than the low-grade ones (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Mann-Whitney U test showed a statistically significant difference between the groups of different grades (p-val=0.04).
source: Mann-Whitney U test showed a statistically significant difference between the groups of different grades (p-val=0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical finding reported in the results.

claim: The higher dispersion of free NAD(P)H fraction in a sample was characteristic of colorectal tumors of early stages (T1, T2) and high grade (G3).
source: Thus, the higher dispersion of free NAD(P)H fraction in a sample was characteristic of colorectal tumors of early stages (T1, T2) and high grade (G3) and thus showed a potential as a prognostic marker.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the data analysis.

claim: The higher dispersion of free NAD(P)H fraction showed a potential as a prognostic marker.
source: Thus, the higher dispersion of free NAD(P)H fraction in a sample was characteristic of colorectal tumors of early stages (T1, T2) and high grade (G3) and thus showed a potential as a prognostic marker.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings suggesting clinical relevance.

claim: Heterogeneity of cellular metabolism increases with model complexity and is the highest at the level of patients' tumors.
source: In the present research, using FLIM of redox cofactor NAD(P)H, which possesses endogenous fluorescence, we compared metabolic features of colorectal cancer cells across in vitro and in vivo models and patients' samples. For the first time, it was shown that heterogeneity of cellular metabolism increases with model complexity and is the highest at the level of patients' tumors.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the study.

claim: The heterogeneity was quantified on the basis of FLIM data and correlated with clinical characteristics of the tumors.
source: The heterogeneity was quantified on the basis of FLIM data and correlated with clinical characteristics of the tumors, which has not been done before.
evidence: This is a description of the study's contribution.

claim: Metabolic heterogeneity was revealed in colorectal cancer cell cultures obtained from the patients' tumors, whereas the cells of the standard cell lines were uniform in their metabolism.
source: Using NAD(P)H FLIM, metabolic heterogeneity was revealed in colorectal cancer cell cultures obtained from the patients' tumors, whereas the cells of the standard cell lines were uniform in their metabolism (Shirshin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: J. Chacko and K. Eliceiri observed intercellular heterogeneity of metabolism in the MCF10A human breast epithelial cell line.
source: J. Chacko and K. Eliceiri observed intercellular heterogeneity of metabolism in the MCF10A human breast epithelial cell line (Chacko and Eliceiri, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Tumor spheroids obtained from the cervical cancer cell line HeLa displayed the differences in metabolism between the outer and the inner cell layers with the outer layers being more glycolytic (higher NAD(P)H-a1).
source: For example, tumor spheroids obtained from the cervical cancer cell line HeLa (Lukina et al., 2018) or murine colorectal carcinoma cell line CT26 (Shirmanova et al., 2021) displayed the differences in metabolism between the outer and the inner cell layers with the outer layers being more glycolytic (higher NAD(P)H-a1).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The spheroids generated from the patients' derived glioblastoma cultures did not show metabolic zonality, but generally had greater intercellular variations of NAD(P)H lifetime parameters than the spheroids from standard line U373 MG.
source: The spheroids generated from the patients' derived glioblastoma cultures did not show metabolic zonality, but generally had greater intercellular variations of NAD(P)H lifetime parameters than the spheroids from standard line U373 MG (Yuzhakova et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The heterogeneous structure of tumor and its microenvironment was shown on PyMT mammary tumors.
source: In the research in vivo, the heterogeneous structure of tumor and its microenvironment was shown on PyMT mammary tumors (Burkel et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Analysis of the optical metabolic parameters revealed heterogeneity of the B78 mouse melanoma model, caused by different microenvironments.
source: Analysis of the optical metabolic parameters revealed heterogeneity of the B78 mouse melanoma model, caused by different microenvironments (Heaton et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Tumor heterogeneity could be induced by such factors as pH, nutrient and oxygen availability, or activation of immune cells.
source: The authors suggested that tumor heterogeneity could be induced by such factors as pH, nutrient and oxygen availability, or activation of immune cells.
evidence: This is cited from the literature as a suggestion from other authors.

claim: Metabolically different cells were detected in the cellular and collagen-rich areas in the in vivo study on HeLa tumor xenografts.
source: In the in vivo study on HeLa tumor xenografts, metabolically different cells were detected in the cellular and collagen-rich areas (Shirmanova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: A high variability of cellular metabolic statuses in CT26 tumors of large size compared with small tumors correlated with heterogeneous oxygen distribution.
source: Recently, we demonstrated a high variability of cellular metabolic statuses in CT26 tumors of large size compared with small tumors, which correlated with heterogeneous oxygen distribution (Parshina et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: A significant intertumor heterogeneity of metabolism was observed in patient-derived glioblastoma xenografts, which differed them from standard U87 glioma.
source: A significant intertumor heterogeneity of metabolism was observed in patient-derived glioblastoma xenografts, which differed them from standard U87 glioma (Yuzhakova et al., 2022).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Colorectal cancer cell lines lack the molecular heterogeneity of clinical colorectal tumors.
source: This result is consistent with the study by J. Auman and H. McLeod using genome-wide gene expression data; the authors concluded that colorectal cancer cell lines lack the molecular heterogeneity of clinical colorectal tumors (Auman and McLeod, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The heterogeneous metabolism after treatment was detected in tumor organoids and in animal models.
source: The heterogeneous metabolism after treatment was detected in tumor organoids (Walsh et al., 2016; Walsh et al., 2014; Gillette et al., 2021) and in animal models (Heaster et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The presence of metabolically distinct cells led to the varying drug responses.
source: In any case, the presence of metabolically distinct cells led to the varying drug responses.
evidence: This is stated as a general conclusion from the cited studies.

claim: Using NAD(P)H FLIM-microscopy of postoperative samples, a high degree of inter- and intratumor heterogeneity of T3 stage colorectal tumors was observed in comparison with normal colon samples.
source: Previously, using NAD(P)H FLIM-microscopy of postoperative samples, we observed a high degree of inter- and intratumor heterogeneity of T3 stage colorectal tumors in comparison with normal colon samples (Lukina et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous work.

claim: The ratio of EpCam- to vimentin-positive cells in patients' samples neither correlated with D-a1 nor with BI-a1.
source: However, the ratio of EpCam- to vimentin-positive cells in patients' samples neither correlated with D-a1 nor with BI-a1, which means that the presence of cells with mesenchymal phenotype did not contribute to metabolic heterogeneity of tumors identified by NAD(P)H FLIM.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: The presence of cells with mesenchymal phenotype did not contribute to metabolic heterogeneity of tumors identified by NAD(P)H FLIM.
source: However, the ratio of EpCam- to vimentin-positive cells in patients' samples neither correlated with D-a1 nor with BI-a1, which means that the presence of cells with mesenchymal phenotype did not contribute to metabolic heterogeneity of tumors identified by NAD(P)H FLIM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data.

claim: Glucose transporter 3 (GLUT3) was highly expressed in colorectal cancer tissues of 63% of patients as relative to benign tissues and correlated with poor clinical outcomes.
source: For example, glucose transporter 3 (GLUT3) was highly expressed in colorectal cancer tissues of 63% of patients as relative to benign tissues and correlated with poor clinical outcomes (Dai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: A sum score based on the expression levels of six proteins (PTEN, p53, GLUT1, PKM2, LDHA, MCT4) in colorectal cancer showed worse survival of patients with a higher probability of the Warburg effect.
source: In the study by Offermans et al., 2022 a sum score based on the expression levels of six proteins (PTEN, p53, GLUT1, PKM2, LDHA, MCT4) in colorectal cancer showed worse survival of patients with a higher probability of the Warburg effect .
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Expression of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) at the invasive margin of the tumor was weaker than in the center.
source: Mizuno et al., 2020 found that expression of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) at the invasive margin of the tumor was weaker than in the center.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Standard molecular genetics and immunolabeling techniques identify the metabolic differences between tumors or between large areas within a tumor, while a single cell level metabolic information is lacking.
source: Note that standard molecular genetics and immunolabeling techniques identify the metabolic differences between tumors or between large areas within a tumor, while a single cell level metabolic information is lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: The expression level of glycolytic enzymes provides some information about intertumor metabolic differences, but is insensitive to intercellular variability of metabolism registered by NAD(P)H FLIM.
source: One can see from representative IHC images that the expression level of glycolytic enzymes provides some information about intertumor metabolic differences, but is insensitive to intercellular variability of metabolism registered by NAD(P)H FLIM (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data comparing IHC with FLIM.

claim: KRAS mutant tumors had more 18F-FDG uptake and heterogeneity than wild-type KRAS.
source: Liu et al. found a correlation between intratumor metabolic heterogeneity parameters of 18F-FDG PET/CT and KRAS mutation status in colorectal cancer – KRAS mutant tumors had more 18F-FDG uptake and heterogeneity than wild-type KRAS (Liu et al., 2022a).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Intratumor metabolic heterogeneity assessed from 18F-FDG PET/CT is an important prognostic factor for progression-free survival and overall survival in patients with colorectal cancer.
source: In a different study they showed that intratumor metabolic heterogeneity assessed from 18F-FDG PET/CT is an important prognostic factor for progression-free survival and overall survival in patients with colorectal cancer (Liu et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: The value of intratumoral metabolic heterogeneity in 18F-FDG PET/CT for prediction of recurrence in patients with locally advanced colorectal cancer was demonstrated.
source: The value of intratumoral metabolic heterogeneity in 18F-FDG PET/CT for prediction of recurrence in patients with locally advanced colorectal cancer was also demonstrated by Han et al., 2018.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Intratumoral metabolic heterogeneity derived from 18F-FDG PET/CT was higher in colorectal tumors with a high microsatellite instability (MSI) and predicted MSI in stage I–III colorectal cancer patients preoperatively.
source: In the study by Zhang et al. intratumoral metabolic heterogeneity derived from 18F-FDG PET/CT was higher in colorectal tumors with a high microsatellite instability (MSI) – an important prognostic biomarker, and predicted MSI in stage I–III colorectal cancer patients preoperatively (Zhang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Patients with a higher metabolic risk score based on genes involved in lipid metabolism pathways had worse prognosis.
source: Lin et al., 2021 identified two subtypes of colorectal cancer using a metabolic risk score based on genes that were mostly involved in lipid metabolism pathways; this criterion was applied for survival prediction – patients with a higher metabolic risk score had worse prognosis.
evidence: This is cited from the literature.

claim: Clinical studies consider intratumor metabolic heterogeneity as a useful prognostic factor.
source: Therefore, these clinical studies consider intratumor metabolic heterogeneity as a useful prognostic factor.
